comparative-advantage-s1.title: Shirts and hats: output per worker

table.caption: Most shirts or hats one worker can make in a day in two invented countries (output data)

comparative-advantage-s2.title: Tables and chairs: hours per unit

table.caption: Hours of labor needed to make one table or one chair in two invented countries (input data)

items.q: Using the table, what is Corvia's opportunity cost of making one hat, in shirts?

why.correct: A Corvian worker who makes 8 hats gives up 24 shirts, so one hat costs $\frac{24}{8} = 3$ shirts.

mistakes.why: That is the cost of one shirt in hats (8 / 24). For one hat, divide the shirts given up by the hats gained: 24 / 8.

items.q: Which country has the absolute advantage in hats?
options: Delmont, because it has the lower opportunity cost of making hats
Corvia, because one worker makes 8 hats a day to Delmont's 6
Delmont, because it makes fewer shirts per worker
Neither, because both countries make hats

why.correct: Absolute advantage means more output from the same resources: 8 hats per worker beats 6.
options: Lower opportunity cost is comparative advantage, not absolute advantage.
Right: more hats from one worker.
Making fewer shirts does not mean making more hats.
Absolute advantage compares how much each makes, and Corvia makes more.

items.q: Which country has the comparative advantage in hats?
options: Delmont, because a hat costs it 2 shirts and costs Corvia 3
Corvia, because each of its workers makes more hats per day
Corvia, because it makes more of both goods
Delmont, because it makes fewer shirts

why.correct: Comparative advantage is the lower opportunity cost. A hat costs Delmont $\frac{12}{6} = 2$ shirts and Corvia 3 shirts.
options: Right: 2 shirts is less than 3.
More hats per worker is absolute advantage.
A country can have the absolute advantage in both goods but the comparative advantage in only one.
The comparison is of opportunity costs, not of shirt output alone.

items.q: If both countries specialize by comparative advantage, what does each produce?
options: Corvia makes both, because it is better at both
Corvia makes hats and Delmont makes shirts
Each makes half of each good
Corvia makes shirts and Delmont makes hats

why.correct: A shirt costs Corvia $\frac{8}{24}$, a third of a hat, and Delmont half a hat, so Corvia specializes in shirts and Delmont in hats.
options: Specializing by absolute advantage misses the gains from trade.
This reverses the comparative advantages.
Splitting production gives up the gains from specializing.
Right: each makes the good with its lower opportunity cost.

items.q: Which terms of trade would benefit both countries?
options: 1 hat for 1.5 shirts
1 hat for 3.5 shirts
1 hat for 2.5 shirts
1 hat for 4 shirts

why.correct: The price of a hat must lie between the two opportunity costs, 2 shirts (Delmont) and 3 shirts (Corvia). Delmont sells hats for more than 2 shirts; Corvia buys them for less than 3.
options: Delmont gives up 2 shirts to make a hat, so selling it for 1.5 loses shirts.
Corvia can make a hat for 3 shirts itself, so it will not pay 3.5.
Right: 2.5 is between 2 and 3.
Corvia can make a hat for 3 shirts itself, so it will not pay 4.

items.q: Using the table, what is Fenwick's opportunity cost of making one table, in chairs?

why.correct: With input data, divide the hours: the 6 hours a table takes could make $\frac{6}{2} = 3$ chairs, so one table costs Fenwick 3 chairs.

mistakes.why: You inverted it, as you would with output data. With hours per unit, a table costs (hours per table) / (hours per chair) = 6 / 2 chairs.

items.q: Which country has the absolute advantage in chairs?
options: Fenwick, because it needs more hours per chair
Ellis, because it needs 1 hour per chair to Fenwick's 2
Fenwick, because it has the lower opportunity cost of chairs
Neither, because both need hours to make chairs

why.correct: With input data, the absolute advantage goes to whoever needs fewer resources per unit: 1 hour beats 2.
options: More hours per unit means less efficient, not more.
Right: fewer hours per chair.
Lower opportunity cost is comparative advantage, not absolute advantage.
Absolute advantage compares the hours needed, and Ellis needs fewer.

items.q: Which country has the comparative advantage in chairs?
options: Fenwick, because a chair costs it a third of a table and costs Ellis half a table
Ellis, because it needs fewer hours per chair
Ellis, because it is faster at both goods
Fenwick, because it needs more hours per table

why.correct: A chair costs Ellis $\frac{1}{2}$ of a table and Fenwick $\frac{2}{6}$, a third of a table, so Fenwick has the lower opportunity cost.
options: Right: a third of a table is less than half.
Fewer hours per chair is absolute advantage.
Being faster at both gives Ellis the absolute advantage in both, not the comparative advantage in both.
Hours per table alone do not give the cost of a chair.

items.q: A student says, "Ellis needs fewer hours for both goods, so trade with Fenwick cannot help Ellis." What is wrong with the claim?
options: Nothing: a country with the absolute advantage in both goods gains nothing from trading with others
Ellis gains if Fenwick also has an absolute advantage in something
Trade helps Ellis if it switches to making chairs
Ellis gains by making tables and buying chairs at a price below its own opportunity cost

why.correct: Gains from trade come from comparative advantage. Ellis gives up 2 chairs per table; if it can get a chair for less than half a table from Fenwick, it ends up with more of both.
options: Both sides can gain whenever their opportunity costs differ.
Absolute advantage is not needed for gains from trade.
Ellis's comparative advantage is in tables, so it gains by making tables.
Right: comparative advantage, not absolute advantage, drives the gains.

items.q: A surgeon types faster than her assistant but pays the assistant to do her typing. Which idea explains this?
options: Absolute advantage: the assistant types faster than the surgeon
Scarcity: there is not enough typing to go around
Comparative advantage: an hour of typing costs the surgeon far more surgery than it costs the assistant
Increasing opportunity cost: typing gets harder the more she does

why.correct: The surgeon has the absolute advantage in typing, but her opportunity cost of typing (surgery not done) is much higher, so the assistant has the comparative advantage in it.
options: The surgeon types faster, so she has the absolute advantage in typing.
The choice is about who should type, not a lack of typing.
Right: the lower opportunity cost belongs to the assistant.
Nothing suggests her typing gets harder; her time is simply worth more in surgery.

items.q: Can one country have the comparative advantage in both of two goods?
options: Yes: if it has the absolute advantage in both
No: if its opportunity cost of one good is lower, its opportunity cost of the other is higher
Yes: if it has more workers
Yes: if its PPC is farther out

why.correct: The opportunity cost of one good is the reciprocal of the opportunity cost of the other, so a lower cost of one means a higher cost of the other.
options: Absolute advantage in both is possible; comparative advantage in both is not.
Right: the two costs are reciprocals.
More workers can give an absolute advantage, not a comparative advantage in both.
A larger PPC shows more output, not lower opportunity costs of both.

items.q: Two countries specialize by comparative advantage and trade at terms between their opportunity costs. Which results follow? Select all that apply.
options: Their combined output of the two goods can rise
Each can consume a combination outside its own PPC
The country with the absolute advantage in both goods gains and the other loses
Each country's PPC shifts outward

why.correct: Specializing raises total output, and trading lets each country consume beyond its own production possibilities. Neither country's ability to produce changes.
options: Right: each makes what it makes at the lower cost.
Right: trade lets consumption go beyond what each could make alone.
At terms between the two costs, both gain.
Trade does not change resources or technology, so the PPCs stay put.

items.q: Two countries have the same opportunity cost of wheat in terms of cloth. What does this imply about trade between them?
options: Neither gains from specializing and trading these goods
Both gain a great deal
The larger country gains and the smaller loses
They gain as long as the terms of trade are set high enough

why.correct: Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity costs. With equal costs, there is no price at which both do better than making the goods themselves.
options: Right: no difference in costs, no gain.
Gains need different opportunity costs.
Size does not create comparative advantage.
With equal costs there is no range between them for the terms of trade.

items.q: Why must mutually beneficial terms of trade lie between the two countries' opportunity costs?
options: The richer country sets the price
Prices in trade are set at the exact average of the two costs
Countries trade goods they are unable to make
Each country must get a good for less than it costs to make at home

why.correct: A country buys a good from abroad only if it pays less than its own opportunity cost, and sells only if it receives more than its own; both conditions hold only between the two costs.
options: Wealth does not set the terms; the opportunity costs do.
Any price between the costs works; the average is one choice.
Countries often trade goods they could make, as the examples show.
Right: both must beat their own opportunity cost.

items.q: In Corvia one worker makes 24 shirts or 8 hats a day. Corvia trades for hats at 1 hat for 2.5 shirts. How many shirts does Corvia save on each hat it buys instead of making it?

why.correct: Making a hat costs Corvia $\frac{24}{8} = 3$ shirts; buying one costs 2.5 shirts, so Corvia saves $3 - 2.5 = 0.5$ shirt per hat.

mistakes.why: That is the price Corvia pays. The gain is its own opportunity cost (3 shirts) minus that price.
That is what a hat costs Corvia to make. The gain is that cost minus the 2.5 shirts it pays.

items.q: Put the steps for finding comparative advantage from an output table in order.
options: Find each country's opportunity cost of each good
Compare the two countries' opportunity costs for each good
Give each good to the country with its lower opportunity cost
Choose terms of trade between the two opportunity costs

why.correct: Costs first, then the comparison, then specialization, then a price between the two costs.
